subject: Immunology
vignette: A 10-day-old neonate is brought for persistent umbilical stump oozing; the cord did not fall off and the area is erythematous and infected. He was delivered at term without complications. He now has a fever with a perirectal abscess and a deep soft tissue infection of the leg. Laboratory studies show marked neutrophilia (absolute neutrophil count 45,000/microliter) that persists even between infections. Pus from the abscess yields no organisms on Gram stain and culture, and the wound does not form a proper collection of pus.
question: Which of the following best explains this presentation?

options.text: Absence of CD18 beta-2 integrin preventing neutrophil adhesion and transmigration
Defective NADPH oxidase with impaired superoxide production
Deficiency of C5-C9 causing recurrent Neisseria infection
Absent T cells with thymic hypoplasia

explanation_correct: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1 is an autosomal recessive deficiency of CD18, the beta-2 integrin chain needed for firm adhesion and transmigration of neutrophils to sites of infection. Patients present in the neonatal period with delayed umbilical cord separation, recurrent bacterial infections without pus formation, and persistent neutrophilia because neutrophils cannot egress from the bloodstream. Neutrophil counts remain high even when the patient is well, a signature finding.

explanation_incorrect.B: Defective NADPH oxidase causes chronic granulomatous disease, which presents later with granulomatous suppurative infections from catalase-positive organisms and normal neutrophil counts.
explanation_incorrect.C: Terminal complement deficiency causes recurrent Neisseria meningitidis infections typically in childhood or adolescence, not this neonatal pattern.
explanation_incorrect.D: Thymic hypoplasia (DiGeorge) causes T-cell lymphopenia and hypocalcemia, which do not explain delayed cord separation or absent pus.
explanation_incorrect.E: Platelets are unaffected in LAD, and the primary defect is in neutrophil integrin function rather than thrombopoiesis.

educationalObjective: LAD type 1 (CD18 deficiency) presents with delayed umbilical cord separation, infections without pus, and persistent neutrophilia.

subject: Immunology
vignette: A 3-year-old boy with silvery-gray hair and light skin presents with recurrent pyogenic infections of the skin and respiratory tract. He has horizontal nystagmus and a history of partial albinism noted at birth. Blood smear shows very large azurophilic granules within neutrophils and lymphocytes. His platelet count, neutrophil count, and immunoglobulin levels are normal. The family reports that a cousin had similar hair and died of an infection-related condition at age 5.
question: Which of the following is the most likely underlying defect and associated complication in this patient?

options.text: Defective CD18 integrin with absent pus formation
Mutation causing impaired lysosomal trafficking with neutropenia, defective chemotaxis, and giant granules; risk of accelerated lymphoproliferative phase
Defective NADPH oxidase with absent porphyrin metabolism
Absent tyrosinase causing albinism without immunodeficiency
Deficiency of the common gamma chain causing NK-cell deficiency

explanation_correct: Chediak-Higashi syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder of lysosomal trafficking (LYST mutation) causing giant lysosomal granules that impair phagolysosome function and cause partial albinism from granule defects in melanocytes. Along with neutropenia and defective chemotaxis, patients experience recurrent pyogenic infections and often develop an accelerated lymphoproliferative phase driven by defective NK-cell function, with hepatosplenomegaly and cytopenias. A classic association is the silvery-gray hair, and the disease is often fatal by childhood without stem cell transplantation.

explanation_incorrect.A: CD18 integrin deficiency is leukocyte adhesion deficiency, which produces delayed cord separation, persistent neutrophilia, and infections without pus, not giant granules or albinism.
explanation_incorrect.C: Chronic granulomatous disease involves NADPH oxidase and does not cause hair or skin pigment changes or giant granules.
explanation_incorrect.D: Oculocutaneous albinism from tyrosinase deficiency causes hypopigmentation alone without recurrent infections or giant granules.
explanation_incorrect.E: Common gamma chain deficiency is X-linked SCID with absent T and NK cells, and it does not produce partial albinism or giant leukocyte granules.

educationalObjective: Chediak-Higashi syndrome (LYST mutation) features partial albinism, giant granulocytes, defective chemotaxis and killing, and an accelerated lymphoproliferative phase.

subject: Immunology
vignette: A 1-day-old infant is evaluated for an umbilical stump that remains attached at 3 weeks of age and is surrounded by erythema with a foul discharge. His mother reports that he was circumcised and the wound oozed for days. Absolute neutrophil count is 38,000/microliter with a left shift, but no neutrophils are seen in the umbilical exudate. Flow cytometry shows absent CD18 on the surface of leukocytes.
question: Which of the following laboratory findings is most characteristic of this patient's diagnosis?

options.text: Absent neutrophils on peripheral blood smear with agranulocytosis
Normal neutrophil counts that fall during infection
Persistently elevated neutrophil count despite infection, with absent neutrophils at the site of infection

explanation_correct: In leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1, absent CD18 prevents neutrophils from adhering to endothelium and crossing into tissues, so they accumulate in the bloodstream and the peripheral count rises, often dramatically, and remains elevated even between infections. Because the cells never reach the tissue, pus is scanty or absent and cultures from the infected site may be sterile. Diagnosis is confirmed by flow cytometry showing absent CD11/CD18 on leukocytes.

explanation_incorrect.A: Peripheral neutrophil counts are markedly elevated in LAD, not absent, because the cells cannot leave the vasculature.
explanation_incorrect.B: Neutrophil counts are persistently high in LAD and do not normalize or fall during infection, which is a key diagnostic clue.
explanation_incorrect.D: Eosinophilia with high IgE suggests hyper-IgE or parasitic disease, not an integrin adhesion defect.
explanation_incorrect.E: Lymphopenia with absent B cells describes Bruton agammaglobulinemia, which has no effect on neutrophil sticking or cord separation.

educationalObjective: LAD type 1 shows persistent neutrophilia with few or no neutrophils at infected sites because CD18-mediated adhesion and transmigration are defective.
